item.aggregated_output: {"id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","track":"held_out","category":"convergent_evolution","prompt":"NAD(P)-binding enzymes occur in multiple SCOP folds and superfamilies. What does this imply about convergent versus divergent evolution, and why is cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone insufficient evidence of homology?"}

item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"NAD- and NADP-dependent enzymes are not a single homologous group in SCOPe. SCOPe contains NAD(P)-binding proteins in more than one fold and in more than one superfamily; a canonical example is the alpha/beta class Rossmann lineage, fold c.2 “NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains”, superfamily c.2.1, but other oxidoreductase and dehydrogenase scaffolds bind the same dinucleotide without being placed in that superfamily. The implication is two-level: members of one SCOPe family or superfamily can be treated as divergent homologs, whereas enzymes that merely bind NAD(P), or that sit in different folds/superfamilies, may be analogous products of repeated recruitment of the same cofactor chemistry. Across different SCOPe folds the evidence for convergence is especially strong because the global topology of the protein scaffold differs; across different superfamilies within a fold, SCOPe is intentionally weaker and says that the shared fold is not by itself enough to prove common ancestry. Cofactor binding alone is weak evidence because NAD(P) presents the same adenosine, ribose, pyrophosphate, nicotinamide, and sometimes 2'-phosphate groups to every enzyme, so unrelated proteins can evolve similar phosphate-binding loops, glycine-rich turns, helix-dipole contacts, and Asp/Glu/Lys/Arg contacts to solve the same local binding problem. Active-site similarity has the same limitation: residues that contact the nicotinamide or perform hydride-transfer chemistry can be placed at locally similar positions by chemical necessity even when the rest of the domain has a different topology. Homology should therefore be supported by global structural alignment, conserved topology, sequence motifs outside the cofactor-binding loop, family/superfamily placement, and ideally phylogenetic or domain-context evidence, not just by seeing NAD(P) in the structure or a few similarly arranged catalytic atoms. The practical limits are important: do not transfer substrate specificity, catalytic residues, oligomeric state, reaction direction, NAD versus NADP preference, or a SCOPe representative assignment across all NAD(P)-binding enzymes. Templates and representatives should normally be chosen within the same family when detailed function is needed and within the same SCOPe superfamily only for broader homology; a template from a different fold or an unrelated NAD(P)-binding superfamily is at most an analog for the cofactor-binding geometry, not evidence of descent from the same ancestor.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
